SELF-EVOLVING AGENTSINTRODUCTION

Why should the next task be easier?

Self-evolution: experience changes retained state that shapes later behavior.

The promise

Finish a task.
Keep what it teaches.
Use that lesson on later work.

The difficulty

A success may be specific to one case.
A failure may leave the wrong lesson.
How do we decide what to keep?

A lesson can change context, software, or weights

Different systems move the boundary between the agent and its learning machinery.

Retained changeWhat changes next timeExamples
Memory / skillsFacts, lessons, executable proceduresVoyager · WikiSkill
Prompt / harnessInstructions and tool orchestrationGEPA
Model weightsThe model’s learned parametersSEAL · R-Zero
Improvement methodHow future changes are proposedSTOP · Hyperagents

Useful learning is established; sustained compounding is not

What we found across the three results sections

01

A useful procedure

Experience helps with later work.

Bounded positive evidence
02

A better improver

Experience helps produce future procedures.

Promising transfer evidence
03

Sustained compounding

Further learning becomes repeatedly more efficient.

Not established

Specialization can be useful learning. Transfer, durability, and cost remain separate questions.

SELF-EVOLVING AGENTSCONCLUSION

Test the next task, the old task, and the bill

Proposed evaluation · commit to the test before optimizing the system

QuestionMeasureLimitation it can reveal
Does it transfer?New task families and a later time periodTransfer limited to familiar tasks
Does it retain?Earlier-task quality and regression countsNew learning that erases old abilities
Does it pay?Search + training + execution + judgingGains bought by hidden computation
Does it repeat?Independent runs and independent evaluationLucky runs or rubric-specific behavior

A rising best score alone establishes neither durable learning nor accelerating improvement.

WHAT THE EVIDENCE SUPPORTS

Make experience valuable beyond its original task

Useful procedures: supported in bounded settings.
Better improvement methods: promising transfer evidence.
Sustained compounding: still to be demonstrated.

Lasting value requires transfer, retention, and full cost accounting.

Appendix · one-shot authoring is a different test

SkillsBench compares agents given curated skill packs, no skills, or one-shot self-authored skills.

Curated skills help on average

Expert procedures are a meaningful baseline for an evolving agent.

Benefits still vary across tasks.

Self-authoring is one-shot here

Three tested configurations underperform no skills.

No repeated outcome-feedback loop: this does not settle iterative learning.

SkillsBench v4: human curation cost and autonomous authoring effort are not matched.

Appendix · editing an agent and editing its improver differ

The important boundary is which learning decisions experience can change.

SystemWhat can changeWhat remains externally specified
SICAAgent implementationExpand the best-scoring agent
DGMAgent code; alternate lineagesImprovement-instruction generator
HyperagentsTask code + improvement codeOuter archive and evaluation

Edit permission makes a hypothesis testable. It does not establish that the edits help.
